summary: Comments on Chuck Holland's proposed Remote Job Entry protocol in RFC 360. The author calls it an excellent document, then offers suggestions and small corrections, such as preferring the command QUIT to BYE and fixing the pathname syntax so host, socket and file names are used consistently across protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone read a draft of the rules for sending jobs and wrote back with friendly tips, like choosing a clearer word for a command.

subtitle: Technical comments on the proposed Remote Job Entry protocol.

tldr.problem: Chuck Holland proposed a Remote Job Entry protocol for running jobs remotely on the ARPANET, but like any new specification, it had room for improvement and consistency.
tldr.mechanism: R.T. Braden from UCLA reviewed the proposal and offered specific suggestions on syntax, error messages, command names and new features such as a transmission status command.
tldr.outcome: The feedback helped refine the protocol before it became a network standard.

today: RFC 368 is a historical record of the peer review process in early network protocol development, showing how feedback improved specifications before standardization.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 368 is a set of comments by R.T. Braden from UCLA on Chuck Holland's proposed Remote Job Entry protocol in RFC 360. Braden calls the proposal excellent and complete, then offers detailed suggestions to improve it before it becomes a network standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone read a draft of new rules for sending computer jobs over the network and wrote back with ideas to make them better.

sections.title: Detailed Suggestions
sections.content:
Braden suggests several improvements: using the command word QUIT instead of BYE for clarity; making the pathname syntax consistent across all network protocols; allowing hexadecimal and octal socket numbers in addition to decimal; extending the syntax to support transmission attributes like TE for EBCDIC; and expanding the code construction to handle multiple varieties of ASCII and EBCDIC.

He also points out that the PORT construction is problematic because it depends on TIP-specific bit conventions, and argues that protocols should not embed hardware-specific details.
sections.plainLanguage: The feedback suggests clearer command names, consistent ways to write addresses, support for different character codes, and avoiding design choices that only work on one type of machine.

sections.title: Operational Experience
sections.content: Braden adds practical observations from running remote jobs at CCN via the ARPANET. He notes that users need a transmission status command to check progress on large jobs, since network bandwidth was limited and the average output job from the network contained about 30 pages, leading to significant delays. He also suggests more specific syntax error messages to help users diagnose what went wrong.
sections.plainLanguage: From experience with real network jobs, people need to check how much data has been sent or received while waiting for a big job to finish.

references.text: Holland, C., "Proposed Remote Job Entry Protocol", RFC 360, June 1972.
